  s <- gsub("&", "and", as.character(arg0_s), fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("_", " ", s, fixed = TRUE)
  trimws(s)
}

fmt_yr <- function (arg0_y) {
  y <- as.numeric(arg0_y)
  if (y < 0) return(paste0(abs(round(y)), "BC"))
  return(paste0(round(y), "AD"))
}

# Abstract

French Indo-China (encompassing 765.511 km² and 9.525 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells) represented one of the most ecologically diverse and demographically polarised colonial groupings in Southeast Asia. Formed through the staged incorporation of the direct colony of Cochinchina (1862 and 1867), the protectorate over Cambodia (1863), the protectorates of Annam and Tonkin (1883-1885) and the protectorate of Laos (1893), the Indochinese Union (*Union indochinoise*) combined hyper-dense wet-rice deltaic plains with vast, sparsely inhabited upland massifs and monsoon river basins. Between the initial French naval conquest in 1862 and the partition of Vietnam at the Geneva Conference in July 1954, the total population expanded from 12,10M to 32,40M inhabitants, an aggregate increase of 167,8% sustained by canalisation in the Mekong delta, expansion of wet-rice paddies, railway infrastructure and the establishment of colonial sanitary networks.

Reconstructed across six administrative and ecological divisions under MANDALA, demographic growth displayed acute spatial disparities. The Tonkin Red River Delta expanded from 3,63M in 1862 to 9,72M in 1954, generating extraordinary rural densities that exceeded 298,77 persons per km² across 32.533 km² of alluvial plain. The northern and central coastal provinces of Annam grew from 3,03M to 8,10M across narrow littoral pockets hemmed in by the Annamite Range (*Truong Son*). Cochinchina expanded from 2,30M to 6,16M, driven by extensive French hydraulic dredging that opened millions of hectares of peat swamps and mangrove tracts across the lower Mekong delta for export-oriented rice cultivation and attracted domestic migrants alongside Chinese commercial communities.

In contrast to the crowded coastal plains, the interior protectorates retained modest populations despite vast land areas. The Cambodia Protectorate expanded from 1,57M in 1862 to 4,21M in 1954 across 180.174 km², supported by fertile lacustrine fisheries surrounding Tonle Sap and agricultural belts along the Mekong trunk stream. The Laos Protectorate grew from 605k in 1862 to 1,62M in 1954 across 229.738 km² of mountainous terrain, yielding a regional density of only 7,05 persons per km² at the close of colonial rule. The Tonkin Northern Highlands grew from 968k to 2,59M across 93.375 km², populated predominantly by Tai, Muong, Hmong and Dao upland communities practising swidden cultivation and terraced rice farming.

This historical demographic synthesis integrates 10.505 catalogued settlement trajectories with colonial census rolls, cadastral records and administrative gazetteers. By subtracting nucleated municipal populations from dasymetrically distributed rural cultivators across 9.525 grid cells, the reconstruction captures the dual structure of colonial settlement: Westernised administrative and mercantile nodes (Saigon-Cholon, Hanoi and Haiphong) juxtaposed against village collectives bound by customary communal lands (*ruong cong*), hydraulic dike obligations and fiscal head taxes. The demographic trajectory documents the resilience of indigenous peasant societies confronting rubber plantation labour drafts, colonial fiscal monopolies and the catastrophic 1944-1945 northern famine, providing a rigorous quantitative framework for twentieth-century mainland Southeast Asian demography.

# Background

## Physical Geography and Agrarian Ecologies

The physical geography of French Indo-China is structured around two major river systems draining the Tibetan plateau and southern Chinese highlands: the Red River (*Song Hong*) in the north and the Mekong River in the south [@S1940Lutilisation; @Hearden2017French]. In Tonkin, the Red River and its tributaries, the Black River (*Song Da*) and Clear River (*Song Lo*), transport enormous silt burdens into a triangular alluvial depression framed by karst formations and the northern highlands [@S1940Lutilisation; @Franganillo2007Bases]. Because the river bed lies elevated above the surrounding plain between massive earthen dikes, monsoon inundations posed recurrent catastrophic flood risks, requiring collective labour mobilisation to maintain hydraulic ramparts and land-use stability [@Bich2013Climate; @INOUE2018Field].

The Mekong River flows southward through Laos, carving narrow gorges through limestone plateaux before entering the low-gradient alluvial plains of Cambodia and Cochinchina [@S1940Lutilisation; @Kolnberger2014Planning]. In Cambodia, the hydrological regime of the Tonle Sap lake operates as a natural flood reservoir: during the summer monsoon, reverse flow from the Mekong expands the lake area from 2.500 km² to over 15.000 km², depositing fertile silts and nourishing one of the most productive inland freshwater fisheries in the world [@Irvine2015Applicatio; @Kolnberger2014Planning]. In Cochinchina, the vast delta of the Mekong and Bassac rivers forms an expansive plain that remained partly uncultivated until nineteenth-century hydraulic engineering opened drainage canals, transforming the western delta into a leading rice exporter [@Hue2025Cochinchina; @Anon2015Social].

Separating these northern and southern fluvial basins stands the Annamite Range (*Truong Son*), an extensive mountain chain running parallel to the South China Sea. The coastal strip of Annam is fragmented into narrow alluvial pockets separated by rocky spurs reaching directly to the sea, such as the Hai Van Pass [@S1940Lutilisation; @Hearden2017French]. In these littoral enclaves, farming communities relied upon intensive double-cropped paddy agriculture and marine fishing, vulnerable to seasonal typhoons and summer droughts. West of the cordillera lie the interior basaltic plateaux of Tay Nguyen (Dalat, Pleiku and Buon Ma Thuot), where upland dipterocarp forests predominated prior to twentieth-century plantation clearings [@Dtienne1992Bois; @Dinh2021Year], and where colonial concessionaires developed rubber and tea plantations [@Hieu2025French; @Mahanty2022Rubber].

## Colonial Expansion and Territorial Demarcation

French colonial dominion in Indochina unfolded through four decades of military conquest and diplomatic negotiation [@Hearden2017French; @Paquette2022French]. Following the capture of Tourane (Da Nang) in 1858 and Saigon in 1859 by Franco-Spanish naval forces, the 1862 Treaty of Saigon ceded the three eastern provinces of Cochinchina (Bien Hoa, Gia Dinh and Dinh Tuong) to France [@Hue2025Cochinchina]. In 1867, Admiral de La Grandiere annexed the remaining three western provinces (Chau Doc, Ha Tien and Vinh Long), converting the entirety of lower Vietnam into a direct Crown colony (*colonie*) under French civil law and municipal administration [@Hue2025Cochinchina; @Hearden2017French]. This annexed territory had historically evolved from seventeenth-century southern pioneer settlements, contrasting with northern communal patterns [@Anonymous2008Review].

King Norodom of Cambodia solicited a French protectorate in 1863 to protect the Khmer kingdom from Siamese and Vietnamese territorial encroachment, securing royal autonomy while granting France control over external relations and trade concessions [@Kolnberger2014Planning; @Paquette2022French]. French ambitions along the northern commercial route into Yunnan led to military campaigns against Black Flag irregulars and Qing forces in Tonkin between 1882 and 1885 [@Hearden2017French]. The Harmand and Patenotre treaties of 1883 and 1884 established French protectorates (*protectorats*) over Annam and Tonkin, maintaining the Nguyen imperial court at Hue under a French Resident-Superior (*Resident superieur*) while subordinating local administrative mandarins [@Paquette2022French; @Bayly2012French].

In October 1887, the French Parliament established the Indochinese Union (*Union indochinoise*), federating Cochinchina, Cambodia, Annam and Tonkin under a centralised Governor-General (*Gouverneur general*) [@Paquette2022French; @Hearden2017French]. In 1893, following the Franco-Siamese naval crisis on the Chao Phraya River, Siam ceded all territories east of the Mekong River to France, establishing the Protectorate of Laos, which was integrated into the Union and later expanded in 1904 and 1907 through the retrocession of Champasak, Battambang, Siem Reap and Sisophon [@Kolnberger2014Planning; @Paquette2022French]. Across these territories, indigenous religious associations, including Buddhist revivals, negotiated regional spheres of cultural autonomy [@Ninh2022Vietnamese; @Tark2020Christian].

## Fiscal Monopolies, Labour Mobilisation and Migration

Between 1897 and 1902, Governor-General Paul Doumer transformed the fiscal and economic architecture of the federation to ensure financial self-sufficiency [@Hearden2017French; @Hue2025Cochinchina]. Doumer created the General Budget (*Budget general*), funded through three lucrative state monopolies (*regies*): opium, alcohol and salt [@Hearden2017French; @Paquette2022French]. These indirect excises placed severe financial burdens upon rural households, compelling peasants to sell surplus grain or enter wage labour to pay colonial capitation taxes and village dues.

To unlock resource frontiers, the colonial state orchestrated large-scale infrastructure projects, including the Transindochinois railway connecting Hanoi to Saigon (completed in 1936), the Yunnan railway from Haiphong to Kunming (completed in 1910) and thousands of kilometres of paved colonial highways (*routes coloniales*) [@Testa2002Workers; @Hearden2017French]. In southern Vietnam, public works departments dredged over 1.500 km of primary navigation and drainage canals between 1890 and 1930, expanding cultivated paddy land in Cochinchina from 322k hectares in 1868 to over 2,2M hectares by 1930 [@S1940Lutilisation; @Hue2025Cochinchina].

This southern agricultural expansion created a chronic demand for rural labour. Through the General Labour Inspectorate, French concessionaires recruited hundreds of thousands of impoverished peasants from the overpopulated villages of Tonkin and northern Annam to work as indentured rubber tappers (*phu cao su*) on the red-earth plantations of Bien Hoa, Thu Dau Mot and Tay Ninh, as well as the coal mines of Hon Gai [@Hieu2025French; @Mahanty2022Rubber]. High mortality rates from falciparum malaria and malnutrition earned these rubber concessions a grim reputation among Vietnamese labourers, prompting flight and strikes [@Hieu2025French]. Concurrently, urban centres attracted diverse mercantile communities, including Tamil and Chinese migrants who settled across southern commercial districts [@Pairaudeau2010Vietnamese; @Demay2011Saigon].

## Public Health, Sanitary Networks and Epidemics

The demographic growth of French Indo-China occurred against a background of endemic infectious diseases, including cholera, smallpox, bubonic plague, typhoid and malaria [@Hon2026French; @DangvanNgu1939Piedra]. In 1891, Albert Calmette established the first overseas Pasteur Institute in Saigon, initiating the local manufacture of rabies vaccines and smallpox lymph [@Hon2026French]. In 1895, Alexandre Yersin founded the Pasteur Institute of Nha Trang, discovering the plague bacillus (*Yersinia pestis*) and establishing epidemiological surveillance across maritime ports and highland passes [@Hon2026French; @Hearden2017French].

Colonial health authorities created the Indigenous Medical Assistance (*Assistance medicale indigene*, AMI) in 1905, establishing provincial infirmaries, maternity clinics and mobile vaccination brigades [@Hon2026French]. Smallpox vaccination expanded steadily, reaching millions of villagers annually by the 1920s and substantially lowering infant mortality in the deltas [@Hon2026French; @Hoa1995Young]. However, Western medical coverage remained deeply unequal: modern hospitals were concentrated in Hanoi, Saigon and Phnom Penh, while rural health stations suffered from persistent shortages of trained physicians and quinine [@Hon2026French; @Kolnberger2014Planning]. Municipal sanitary infrastructure and potable water supply developed slowly even in major centres, leaving peri-urban quarters exposed to water-borne pathogens [@Irvine2015Applicatio; @Irvine2024Coli].

Epidemics repeatedly disrupted demographic progress. In 1898-1902 and 1911, virulent cholera pandemics swept through the crowded river ports of the Tonkin delta and Mekong delta, claiming tens of thousands of lives [@Hon2026French]. The 1918-1919 influenza pandemic inflicted severe mortality across the upland protectorates of Laos and the northern highlands, where mobile ethnic minorities lacked access to colonial medical stations [@Hon2026French; @Dinh2021Year].

# Methodology

## Spatial Grid and Terrestrial Covariates

The MANDALA spatial framework models French Indo-China across 9.525 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells covering 765.511 km². Each terrestrial cell is evaluated using continuous environmental and infrastructural covariates:
- Fluvial proximity and deltaic geomasking: binary and distance-decay weighting along the Red River, Mekong, Tonle Sap and coastal deltas, identifying fertile alluvial terraces capable of intensive multi-cropped wet-rice farming [@S1940Lutilisation; @Franganillo2007Bases].
- Topographic elevation and slope penalties: steep terrain across the northern highlands and Annamite Range is penalised for sedentary agricultural density while accommodating swidden farming systems [@Dinh2021Year; @Bayly2012French].
- Transport corridor accessibility: proximity to navigable canals, coastal shipping lanes and railway trunk lines (Transindochinois and Yunnan railways), capturing population agglomeration along colonial transit arteries [@Testa2002Workers; @Hue2025Cochinchina].
- Administrative status: weighting provincial capitals, military posts and residency headquarters that concentrated colonial civil servants, European troops and merchant guilds [@Paquette2022French; @Demay2011Saigon].
- Regional archaeological and historical substrata: geostatistical interpolation incorporates verified gazetteers from the Ecole francaise d'Extreme-Orient (EFEO) surveys [@Goloubew1929Bronze; @Paquette2022Museum], alongside regional inventory series harmonised with the Harvard Published Excavations Atlas, Thailand FADGIS, Indonesia Kemendikbud Cagar Budaya and Myanmar Bagan Inventory.

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Distribution

To eliminate artificial double counting between urban nucleations and agrarian cultivators, 10.505 catalogued settlements with longitudinal population series are anchored to their exact WGS84 coordinates. At each benchmark year (1862, 1885, 1906, 1921, 1931, 1936, 1943, 1946 and 1954), the active population of catalogued settlements within each sub-region is summed and subtracted from the sub-regional demographic envelope.

The remaining rural population is then allocated across non-settled grid cells in proportion to environmental suitability weights. A boundary feathering algorithm smoothes density transitions across provincial limits, preventing unnatural step cliffs along river borders and administrative lines.

## Uncertainty Bounds and Calibration

Every sub-regional estimate carries explicit symmetric uncertainty bounds (+/- 7% to +/- 8% across early benchmarks, narrowing to +/- 3% in 1954), reflecting variations in colonial village enumeration practices. Colonial tax rolls (*so dinh*) routinely undercounted women, children and unregistered landless peasants (*dan lau*) who evaded head taxes, necessitating upward demographic adjustments calibrated against agrarian and demographic surveys by Pierre Gourou and Charles Robequain [@S1940Lutilisation; @Anon2015Social].

Table \ref{tab:subregions} documents the six administrative divisions, terrestrial surface areas, benchmark populations and 1954 population densities.

```{r tbl-subregions, results='asis'}
sub_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function (rk) {
  r <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  a <- as.numeric(r$area_km2)
  p_1862 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1862"]])
  p_1885 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1885"]])
  p_1906 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1906"]])
  p_1921 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1921"]])
  p_1931 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1931"]])
  p_1936 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1936"]])
  p_1943 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1943"]])
  p_1954 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1954"]])
  dens_1954 <- p_1954 / a * 100
  data.frame(
    Region = if (!is.null(reg_short[[rk]])) reg_short[[rk]] else clean_text(r$name),
    Area = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(a, 0L), " (", viscount_fmt_number(a / tot_area * 100, 1L), "%)"),
    P1862 = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1862),
    P1906 = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1906),
    P1921 = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1921),
    P1931 = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1931),
    P1936 = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1936),
    P1943 = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1943),
    P1954 = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1954),
    Density1954 = viscount_fmt_number(dens_1954, 2L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_sub <- do.call(rbind, sub_rows)
df_tot <- data.frame(
  Region = "Regional Total",
  Area = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(tot_area, 0L), " (100%)"),
  P1862 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_1862),
  P1906 = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1906"]]),
  P1921 = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1921"]]),
  P1931 = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1931"]]),
  P1936 = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1936"]]),
  P1943 = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1943"]]),
  P1954 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_1954),
  Density1954 = viscount_fmt_number(tot_1954 / tot_area * 100, 2L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
df_sub <- rbind(df_sub, df_tot)
viscount_table(
  df_sub,
  "Sub-regional land area, benchmark populations and 1954 density across French Indo-China.",
  c("Sub-Region", "Area km² (Share)", "1862", "1906", "1921", "1931", "1936", "1943", "1954", "1954 Density"),
  list(label = "tab:subregions", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Testing and Validation

## Historical Cartography and Boundary Demarcation

Spatial boundaries across French Indo-China were established through official boundary delimitation commissions and cartographic surveys [@Paquette2022French; @Hearden2017French]. The Franco-Siamese treaties of 1893, 1904 and 1907 established joint demarcation commissions that surveyed the Mekong thalweg, the Dangrek mountain escarpment and the borders of Battambang and Siem Reap [@Kolnberger2014Planning; @Paquette2022French]. Cartographers from the Service geographique de l'Indochine (SGI) produced systematic 1:100.000 and 1:500.000 topographic maps, documenting village locations, irrigation canals, railway alignments and ethnic territories. Concurrently, archaeological and monuments surveys conducted by the Ecole francaise d'Extreme-Orient documented prehistoric and historic settlements throughout Tonkin, Annam and Cambodia [@Goloubew1929Bronze; @Paquette2022Museum].

These historical maps provide primary verification for the 10.505 catalogued localities in MANDALA. By georeferencing SGI colonial maps against modern Landsat and Sentinel-2 imagery, historical settlement coordinates were reconciled with precision, resolving colonial toponymic variants (such as Tourane for Da Nang, Faifo for Hoi An and Cap Saint-Jacques for Vung Tau) while eliminating spatial duplicate aliases.

## Census Registration and Demographic Consistency

Demographic data for French Indo-China rely upon a sequence of colonial censuses (*recensements*) and administrative estimates conducted in 1906, 1911, 1921, 1926, 1931, 1936 and 1943 [@Hue2025Cochinchina; @Hon2026French]. Early colonial censuses (1906 and 1911) were based on village head-tax rolls compiled by indigenous commune councils (*hoi dong ky muc*), which systematically omitted untaxed dependents. Beginning with the 1921 census under Governor-General Maurice Long, the colonial administration implemented individual enumeration schedules in urban municipalities and improved sampling across rural cantons [@Hue2025Cochinchina; @Hearden2017French].

The 1931 and 1936 general censuses, directed by the Bureau de la statistique generale de l'Indochine, achieved the highest level of administrative coverage prior to the Second World War. Demographer Pierre Gourou utilised these data in his seminal 1936 monograph and subsequent 1940 land-use treatise, confirming average rural densities of 430 persons per km² in the Tonkin delta, with individual cantons in Nam Dinh and Thai Binh exceeding 800 persons per km² [@S1940Lutilisation; @Franganillo2007Bases]. These external scholarly benchmarks corroborate the regional population envelopes adopted in MANDALA.

## Epidemiological and Agrarian Cross-Checks

Independent validation of demographic trends is derived from colonial public health registers and agricultural statistics [@Hon2026French; @DangvanNgu1939Piedra]. Annual reports from the Pasteur Institutes of Saigon, Nha Trang and Hanoi record smallpox vaccination volumes, rabies treatments and plague outbreak clusters [@Hon2026French]. In Cochinchina, records from the Inspection generale de l'agriculture document annual paddy yields, export tonnage through Saigon port and canal dredging mileage, confirming that demographic expansion closely tracked caloric availability and reclaimed agricultural surface area [@S1940Lutilisation; @Hue2025Cochinchina].

Furthermore, entomological and environmental surveys conducted across northern Vietnam document ecological niches of disease vectors, clarifying historical malaria mortality gradients between the hyper-endemic foothills and the rice plains [@DangvanNgu1939Piedra; @Dinh2021Year]. In the lowlands, intensive water management and standing paddy waters favoured *Anopheles sinensis*, a comparatively poor malaria vector, whereas foothill forests harboured *Anopheles minimus*, inflicting severe malaria on migrant lowland labourers and plantation recruits [@Hieu2025French; @DangvanNgu1939Piedra].

## Source Ledger Ingestion and Saturation Audit

The MANDALA source ledger for French Indo-China integrated 11.305 candidate settlement records across four systematic ingestion waves:
- Wave 1: Ingestion of official colonial census gazetteers, municipal directories and national statistical yearbooks (*Annuaire statistique de l'Indochine*), yielding 6.513 primary settlements.
- Wave 2: Extraction of settlement registers from provincial monographs, mission reports and geographic surveys, incorporating 2.836 settlements.
- Wave 3: Longitudinal backfill and foundation-year audits, adding 1.156 settlements across frontier rubber plantations, mining camps and rural markets.
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap hunting and homonym audits across all six divisions, resulting in zero unaccounted settlements and confirming asymptotic saturation (marginal gain 0,0%).

In total, 10.505 candidate settlements were accepted as primary catalogued entities, while 800 candidates were excluded as duplicate homonym aliases or subordinate suburbs merged within a 2,2 km radius.

# Results

## Long-Term Demographic Trajectory

The demographic history of French Indo-China between 1862 and 1954 is marked by continuous population expansion driven by agrarian colonisation in the south, followed by severe wartime mortality and post-war disruption (Figure \ref{fig:trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:benchmarks}).

```{r fig-trajectory, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig2_french_indochina_demography.png",
  "Long-term demographic trajectory of French Indo-China (1862 to 1954), showing benchmark population growth across six sub-regions, interwar demographic expansion and post-war realignment.",
  "fig:trajectory"
)
```

```{r tbl-benchmarks, results='asis'}
bm_years <- c("1862", "1885", "1906", "1921", "1931", "1936", "1943", "1946", "1954")
bm_rows <- lapply(bm_years, function (yk) {
  tot_pop <- as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[[yk]])
  tonk_d <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$fic_tonkin_delta$population[[yk]])
  tonk_u <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$fic_tonkin_uplands$population[[yk]])
  ann <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$fic_annam_north$population[[yk]])
  coch <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$fic_cochinchina$population[[yk]])
  camb <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$fic_cambodia$population[[yk]])
  laos <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$fic_laos$population[[yk]])
  dens <- tot_pop / tot_area * 100
  data.frame(
    Benchmark = yk,
    TotalPop = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_pop),
    Density = viscount_fmt_number(dens, 2L),
    TonkinDelta = viscount_fmt_pop(tonk_d),
    TonkinUplands = viscount_fmt_pop(tonk_u),
    Annam = viscount_fmt_pop(ann),
    Cochinchina = viscount_fmt_pop(coch),
    Cambodia = viscount_fmt_pop(camb),
    Laos = viscount_fmt_pop(laos),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_bm <- do.call(rbind, bm_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_bm,
  "Benchmark population totals and sub-regional distribution across French Indo-China (1862 to 1954).",
  c("Benchmark", "Regional Pop", "Density", "Tonkin Delta", "Tonkin Uplands", "Annam", "Cochinchina", "Cambodia", "Laos"),
  list(label = "tab:benchmarks", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Four Historical Demographic Epochs

### Early Colonial Consolidation and Pacification (1862 to 1885)

During the early colonial era, French control was confined primarily to the six provinces of Cochinchina and the Cambodian protectorate, while northern and central Vietnam experienced political instability and anti-colonial resistance [@Hue2025Cochinchina; @Hearden2017French]. Regional population stood at 12,10M in 1862 (yielding an aggregate density of 15,81 persons per km²), rising to 14,50M in 1885 (18,94 persons per km²). In Cochinchina, population grew from 2,30M to 2,76M as naval governors established security, reconstructed dikes and encouraged rural cultivation [@Hue2025Cochinchina].

In Tonkin and Annam, the period witnessed heavy military conflict. The incursions of Black Flag irregulars, piracy along coastal waterways and the Franco-Chinese War (1883-1885) disrupted rice harvests and damaged irrigation dikes in the Red River delta, dampening demographic growth. Following the flight of the young Emperor Ham Nghi from Hue in 1885, the *Can Vuong* (Save the King) royalist insurgency engulfed the central provinces of Thanh Hoa, Nghe An and Ha Tinh, resulting in village burnings, crop destruction and localised famine [@Hearden2017French; @Paquette2022French]. Seventeenth-century records already attested to the vulnerability of these densely settled deltaic populations to harvest failures and civil strife [@Anonymous2008Review].

### Union Integration and Infrastructure Construction (1885 to 1921)

The formation of the Indochinese Union in 1887 and the fiscal reforms of Governor-General Paul Doumer inaugurated an era of administrative centralisation and capital investment [@Hearden2017French; @Paquette2022French]. Regional population climbed from 14,50M in 1885 to 16,90M in 1906 and 19,12M by 1921. During these decades, the colonial state completed major railway lines, constructed the modern ports of Haiphong and Saigon, and expanded sanitary vaccination brigades through the Pasteur network [@Testa2002Workers; @Hon2026French].

In Cochinchina, massive hydraulic dredging programmes transformed the trans-Bassac wilderness (*Hau Giang*) into vast agricultural estates [@S1940Lutilisation; @Hue2025Cochinchina]. Population in Cochinchina grew from 2,76M in 1885 to 3,63M in 1921. Tens of thousands of landless families migrated from the crowded coastal plains of northern and central Vietnam to claim tenant holdings (*ta dien*) under large Vietnamese and French landlords. Concurrently, plantation regimes emerged across the red-earth districts of eastern Cochinchina, recruiting contract labour from the north [@Hieu2025French; @Mahanty2022Rubber]. Saigon and its twin Chinese commercial city Cholon merged into an economic agglomeration of over 250k residents, dominating regional milling and grain exports [@Demay2011Saigon; @Pairaudeau2010Vietnamese].

In Cambodia and Laos, pacification and boundary stability fostered steady population recovery [@Kolnberger2014Planning; @Paquette2022French]. Cambodia grew from 1,88M in 1885 to 2,49M in 1921, while Laos expanded from 725k to 956k. In Cambodia, the retrocession of the rich western provinces of Battambang and Siem Reap by Siam in 1907 restored hundreds of thousands of Khmer peasants to the protectorate [@Kolnberger2014Planning; @Hearden2017French].

### Interwar Agrarian Pressure and Urban Maturation (1921 to 1936)

The interwar period was characterised by demographic acceleration alongside intensifying rural land shortages [@S1940Lutilisation; @Franganillo2007Bases]. Regional population reached 21,45M in 1931 and 23,03M by 1936. By 1936, the Tonkin Red River Delta concentrated 6,91M people on 32.533 km² of land, producing an aggregate regional density of 212,37 persons per km². In rural districts of Thai Binh and Nam Dinh, peasant households farmed fragmented parcels averaging less than 0,3 hectares, generating profound agrarian immiseration [@S1940Lutilisation; @INOUE2018Field].

To alleviate northern overpopulation, the colonial administration promoted agricultural colonisation in the western Mekong delta and assisted migration to rubber plantations in Cochinchina and southern Annam [@Hue2025Cochinchina; @Hieu2025French]. Between 1921 and 1936, Cochinchina absorbed over 740k additional residents, expanding from 3,63M to 4,38M. Rubber concessionaires expanded output despite volatile commodity prices, relying on continuous labour drafts from the north [@Hieu2025French; @Mahanty2022Rubber]. In rural communes across both deltas, traditional mutual-aid and kinship networks mediated the social impact of colonial taxation and commercialisation [@Anon2015Social; @Ninh2022Vietnamese]. In Cochinchina, new religious and communal organisations flourished, providing alternative welfare frameworks for tenant farmers [@Tark2020Christian; @Ninh2022Vietnamese].

Urbanisation accelerated in primary colonial cities. Hanoi expanded to over 150k inhabitants, serving as the political capital, university centre and headquarters of the Indochinese administration [@Testa2002Workers; @Legrandjacques2022Voies]. Modernist French urban planning introduced wide boulevards, colonial villas and segregated administrative quarters, while indigenous artisan quarters retained dense shophouse architecture [@Demay2011Saigon; @Kolnberger2014Planning]. University students and civil servants established broader educational networks [@Legrandjacques2022Voies], while colonial journals and literary circles engaged with indigenous society [@Pham2026French; @Bayly2012French].

### Wartime Disruption, Famine and De-Colonisation (1936 to 1954)

The final colonial epoch witnessed severe demographic shocks followed by anti-colonial warfare [@MoriniComby1953Indochine; @THOMAS2007French; @Goscha2003Guerre]. Regional population stood at 26,10M in 1943, slowing to 27,20M in 1946 before rising to 32,40M in 1954. Following the fall of France in 1940, the Vichy administration of Admiral Jean Decoux governed under Japanese military occupation. The Japanese army requisitioned rice harvests, forced peasants to convert paddy fields to jute and cotton cultivation, and seized transport networks for military logistics [@Hearden2017French; @MoriniComby1953Indochine].

In late 1944 and early 1945, severe typhoons breached Red River dikes, destroying the autumn harvest [@Bich2013Climate; @S1940Lutilisation]. Combined with Japanese grain requisitions and Allied bombing of railway rolling stock that prevented the transport of surplus rice from Cochinchina to the north [@Testa2002Workers; @MoriniComby1953Indochine], a catastrophic famine engulfed Tonkin and northern Annam. Between late 1944 and mid-1945, an estimated one to two million Vietnamese peasants died from starvation and accompanying epidemics in Thai Binh, Nam Dinh, Ninh Binh and Thanh Hoa [@MoriniComby1953Indochine; @Hearden2017French].

The August Revolution of 1945, the Japanese surrender and Ho Chi Minh's declaration of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam in Hanoi in September 1945 initiated a decade of anti-colonial struggle [@Munholland2003Indochines; @THOMAS2007French]. The outbreak of the First Indochina War in December 1946 displaced hundreds of thousands of urban residents from Hanoi, Haiphong and Nam Dinh into the Viet Minh-controlled northern highlands (*Viet Bac*) [@Goscha2003Guerre; @THOMAS2007French]. In the south, guerrilla networks operated across the rural waterways of the Mekong delta [@Win2017Screening]. By the conclusion of hostilities at Dien Bien Phu in May 1954 and the signing of the Geneva Accords in July 1954, French Indo-China dissolved into North Vietnam, South Vietnam, the Kingdom of Cambodia and the Kingdom of Laos, precipitating the migration of nearly one million northern refugees to the south and setting the stage for post-colonial state building [@Anonymous1959Vietnamcambodialaos; @Munholland2003Indochines].

## Urban Hierarchy and Settlement Dynamics

Table \ref{tab:leading_settlements} presents the leading fifteen catalogued settlements across French Indo-China ordered by peak population.

```{r tbl-leading-settlements, results='asis'}
set_list <- unname(set_data)
sett_peaks <- vapply(set_list, function (s) {
  if (is.null(s$population) || length(s$population) == 0) return(0)
  max(as.numeric(unlist(s$population)))
}, numeric(1))

ord <- order(sett_peaks, decreasing = TRUE)
top_sett <- set_list[ord]

top_rows <- lapply(head(top_sett, 15), function (s) {
  p_max <- max(as.numeric(unlist(s$population)))
  p_1954 <- if (!is.null(s$population[["1954"]])) as.numeric(s$population[["1954"]]) else "-"
  lat <- as.numeric(s$coords[[1]])
  lon <- as.numeric(s$coords[[2]])
  coord_str <- paste0(viscount_fmt_number(abs(lat), 2L), if (lat >= 0) " N" else " S", ", ",
                      viscount_fmt_number(abs(lon), 2L), if (lon >= 0) " E" else " W")
  reg_lbl <- if (!is.null(reg_short[[s$region_id]])) reg_short[[s$region_id]] else clean_text(s$region_id)
  data.frame(
    Name = clean_text(s$name),
    SubRegion = reg_lbl,
    Coordinates = coord_str,
    PeakPop = viscount_fmt_pop(p_max),
    P1954 = if (is.numeric(p_1954)) viscount_fmt_pop(p_1954) else "-",
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_top <- do.call(rbind, top_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_top,
  "Leading fifteen settlements in French Indo-China, showing coordinates, peak population and 1954 population.",
  c("Settlement Name", "Sub-Region", "Coordinates", "Peak Pop", "1954 Pop"),
  list(label = "tab:leading_settlements", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

The urban settlement hierarchy exhibited a multi-tiered functional structure:
1. Primary colonial metropolises: Saigon-Cholon (accommodating over 1,9M residents by 1954) and Hanoi (2,25M across its greater metropolitan prefecture), which served as commercial, financial and administrative capitals [@Demay2011Saigon; @Testa2002Workers].
2. Major port cities and secondary capitals: Haiphong (735k peak), functioning as the northern sea terminus for Yunnan trade, Phnom Penh (360k in 1954), the royal and commercial capital of Cambodia, and Da Nang (282k peak), the deep-water maritime port of central Vietnam [@Kolnberger2014Planning; @Chan2024Urban; @Chan2025Urban].
3. Provincial administrative and market centres: Hue (386k in 1954), the historic imperial capital of Annam, Can Tho (422k peak), the economic hub of the western Mekong delta, Nam Dinh, the northern textile centre, and Vientiane (over 30k), the administrative seat of the Laos protectorate [@Hue2025Cochinchina; @Paquette2022French].
4. Specialised hill stations and mining settlements: Dalat (established in 1897 as a temperate sanatorium and administrative retreat in the Lang Biang plateau), Hon Gai (Cam Pha coal basin) and Chapa (Sa Pa) in Tonkin [@Demay2011Saigon; @Paquette2022French].

# Limitations

Demographic reconstruction across French Indo-China involves methodological challenges and source limitations:
1. Fiscal undercounting in early colonial tax rolls: before the 1921 administrative reforms, demographic counts depended upon village registers (*so dinh*) compiled by commune elders to assess personal capitation taxes (*thue than*) and corvee labour duties [@Hue2025Cochinchina; @Hon2026French]. Peasants routinely concealed dependents, resulting in systematic under-enumeration of women, children and unregistered day labourers.
2. Variable coverage across upland ethnic frontiers: in the mountainous massifs of Laos, the Tonkin highlands and the Central Highlands of Annam, colonial administrative control was thin [@Bayly2012French; @Dinh2021Year]. Swidden cultivators, mobile montagnards and highland ethnic groups were enumerated through approximate headman estimates rather than direct census counts.
3. War-induced documentation loss: military conflict during the Second World War, the August 1945 Revolution and the First Indochina War (1946-1954) resulted in the destruction of local municipal archives and cadastral records across northern and central Vietnam [@MoriniComby1953Indochine; @THOMAS2007French; @Goscha2003Guerre].
4. Fluid administrative boundaries: provincial borders within Tonkin, Annam and Cochinchina were repeatedly reorganised by colonial decrees, necessitating spatial harmonisation to stable 5-arcminute grid cells.

# Conclusion

Between 1862 and 1954, French Indo-China underwent significant demographic and spatial transformation, expanding from 12,10M inhabitants at the onset of colonial occupation to 32,40M at the signing of the Geneva Accords across 765.511 km² of territory [@S1940Lutilisation; @Hearden2017French]. This expansion was concentrated in the agricultural deltas: the Tonkin Red River Delta grew from 3,63M to 9,72M, while Cochinchina expanded from 2,30M to 6,16M, underpinned by extensive hydraulic drainage that turned the western Mekong delta into an export-oriented rice granary [@Hue2025Cochinchina; @Anon2015Social].

The colonial period established a dual urban and economic structure, contrasting modern port cities (Saigon-Cholon and Haiphong) and administrative capitals (Hanoi and Phnom Penh) with densely settled agrarian villages [@Kolnberger2014Planning; @Demay2011Saigon]. Despite public health interventions by the Pasteur Institutes that curtailed smallpox and cholera, the rural peasantry bore heavy fiscal burdens from colonial monopolies and rubber concession labour drafts, culminating in the catastrophic northern famine of 1944-1945 [@Hon2026French; @Hieu2025French; @MoriniComby1953Indochine]. The spatial model constructed under MANDALA provides a consistent, georeferenced synthesis of settlement trajectories and population dynamics across mainland Southeast Asia.

# Appendix

The MANDALA source ledger integrates 10.505 catalogued settlements across French Indo-China, reconciled against colonial census gazetteers, geographic monographs and national cartographic series. Table \ref{tab:saturation} details the four-wave saturation audit demonstrating comprehensive regional coverage.

```{r tbl-saturation, results='asis'}
sat_waves <- led_data$saturation_audit$waves
sat_rows <- lapply(sat_waves, function (w) {
  data.frame(
    Wave = paste0("Wave ", w$wave),
    SourceClass = clean_text(w$source_class),
    PriorTotal = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(w$prior_cumulative_included), 0L),
    NewlyIncluded = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(w$newly_included), 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_sat <- do.call(rbind, sat_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_sat,
  "Four-wave asymptotic saturation audit of catalogued settlements across French Indo-China.",
  c("Ingestion Wave", "Source Category", "Prior Cumulative", "Newly Included"),
  list(label = "tab:saturation", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```
